input: This worked example considers a continuous stirred-tank reactor, commonly referred to as a CSTR, which is being used to carry out a hydrolysis reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant. At the operating temperature, the rate constant for the reaction has a value of 0.279 min-1, and the mean residence time of the material inside the reactor is 86 min. When these values are applied to the ideal CSTR model, the steady-state conversion that is obtained is 96%, which represents a very high degree of conversion of the limiting reactant. It is worth bearing in mind, however, that this estimate is built on a set of idealising assumptions, in particular the assumption of perfect mixing throughout the vessel and the assumption that the density of the reacting mixture remains constant. In practice, real vessels can depart from this ideal behaviour, and it should be noted that tracer tests, which would reveal how the actual vessel behaves, have not been run on the vessel in question. The figure of 96% should therefore be understood as the conversion predicted for an ideal CSTR under the stated conditions, rather than as a measured performance figure for the real equipment.
target: Conversion in a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) running a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant is 96% at steady state. The rate constant (0.279 min-1 at the operating temperature) and the mean residence time (86 min) set the result: for first-order kinetics in an ideal CSTR, a rate constant and a residence time of this size leave only a small fraction of the limiting reactant unconverted, and the steady-state conversion follows from the two values together. Conversion here is the fraction of the limiting reactant consumed between the reactor inlet and the reactor outlet. Two assumptions carry the estimate. Mixing is taken as perfect, so the composition everywhere in the vessel equals the outlet composition, and the density is taken as constant along the reaction path. Perfect mixing is a statement about the vessel rather than the reaction: the incoming feed is dispersed through the vessel contents at once, and no part of the vessel holds material of a different age or composition from any other part. Both assumptions are built into the ideal CSTR model behind the estimate. Against the actual vessel, the estimate is unchecked. Tracer tests on the vessel have not been run, so its residence time distribution is unmeasured and any departure from perfect mixing is unknown. The 96% conversion is valid for the ideal CSTR at the stated rate constant and residence time; the conversion of the installed vessel stands or falls with mixing behaviour that has not been measured.
